We rely on a feedback loop: retailers telling us what to cover, brands telling us what to cover, and consumer submissions saying we're missing a new strain. Being digital also means we see search data — not flashy activations, but what's trending in Google search — so we can react accordingly.

I'm Asian, I can't process alcohol well, so a micro-dose cannabis or hemp product appeals to me. We saw huge engagement around content like weed cocktails you can make yourself or where to pick them up, and because of Leafly's authority, we can then go create content — like our top five weed drinks — that opens up placement opportunities for brands.

Bryan Fields: So to make sure I understand — it's January, 'Cali sober' is trending, an article on the top five cannabis beverages goes up, and that creates five brand placement opportunities plus a valuable ad spot next to it for someone looking to buy a hemp beverage?

We've done that throughout the year with edibles for sleep, our drinks content, and more — blending conversations across THC and hemp, since there are different business models when working in a federally legal space versus not. Bryan Fields: What question do you wish more people asked you?

Yoko Miyashita: On behalf of Leafly, I wish people asked more about why Leafly is necessary for this space — because answering that opens up the history of this plant: the cultural, historical, and medicinal foundations, the hundred-year war to suppress it, and the journey of legalizing and reintroducing it. Without appreciating that history, you can't understand why it's so hard for a retailer, a brand, or a consumer, and why a company like Leafly is necessary to help solve those challenges. Personally, I've said before that I admire former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi, particularly how she led a major soda company through the transition brought on by the war on sugar — carrying a brand and an organization through a real mindset shift. We're in the business of changing hearts and minds too, and I want to learn how to inspire people through that kind of transformation.

Bryan Fields: Prediction time — with Leafly's unique position as a marketplace, what emerging consumer trend do you foresee shifting minds?

Yoko Miyashita: Changing the law is a critical part of changing stigma. Just before 4/20 this spring I was in Germany right as they went legal in a limited way starting in April — it'll be slow and messy, but think about the significance of Germany going legal and what dominoes that tips internationally. We'll get there when all fifty states have legal access and there's international acknowledgment that we should get this plant into the hands of the people who can use it safely. It's a hearts-and-minds game, paired with education at every step of the journey.

Kellen Finney: I'll take a similar approach, but I'd point to hemp beverages — most people who consume something mind-altering do it through a beverage or something they eat, and hemp has found a way to deliver Delta-9 THC to any consumer in any state, right to their doorstep. That gives people on the fence about legalization a safe way to try it at home, which will ultimately help prove that this isn't the 'devil's lettuce' it was made out to be for a hundred years.

Bryan Fields: My prediction is personalization — the moment we get first-person data so I can get products tailored for creativity, sleep, exercise, or relaxation, with a known and repeatable outcome, that will be a game changer. I think Leafly has a tremendous first-person data advantage given its status in the industry, and I'm excited to see how personalization unfolds.

Yoko Miyashita: I appreciate that, Bryan — that's spot on. Trust and education really depend on the information we get back from this community, and the willingness of the people who sustain Leafly to share their experiences, which becomes the foundation for building personalization engines we can keep iterating on.

Bryan Fields: Yoko, for our listeners who want to get in touch or learn more, where can they find you?

Yoko Miyashita: First and foremost, leafly.com — download our app on both the Google Play Store and the App Store. I'm also active on LinkedIn and on X. Send me a message, I'd love to hear from you.

Bryan Fields: Thanks for taking the time, this was a lot of fun.
summary: In this episode of The Dime, Leafly CEO Yoko Miyashita joins hosts Bryan Fields and Kellen Finney to explain how Leafly uses a real-time feedback loop from retailers, brands, and consumer submissions to spot emerging cannabis trends like hemp-derived beverages and 'Cali sober' culture. The conversation covers Leafly's education-first mission, the messy divide between regulated cannabis and hemp-derived THC products, the challenges of building trust and clean product data in a state-by-state legal patchwork, and why licensing enough legal retail access — paired with consumer education — is key to beating the illicit market. It's a useful listen for anyone trying to understand how cannabis brands and retailers can navigate compliance, hemp competition, and shifting consumer behavior.
takeaways: Leafly relies on a feedback loop of retailers, brands, and direct consumer submissions to identify trending strains, products, and content gaps.
Search and behavioral data (not big flashy marketing activations) drive Leafly's understanding of emerging consumer trends like hemp beverages and sleep-focused products.
The 'Cali sober' trend and interest in low-dose social alternatives to alcohol has fueled major growth in hemp- and cannabis-derived beverages.
Clean, consistent product data (cannabinoid content, terpenes, batch consistency) remains an unsolved foundational problem for cannabis e-commerce.
Budtenders are a critical trust intermediary between consumers and complex cannabis products, which is why Leafly invests in International Budtender Day and budtender-focused initiatives.
Non-plant-touching cannabis media companies face major restrictions on platforms like Meta/Instagram despite illicit sellers openly operating there.

The regulatory divide between hemp-derived THC products (federally legal, can ship direct-to-consumer) and state-licensed cannabis (heavily regulated, no interstate shipping) creates consumer confusion and competitive tension.
Consumers largely make cannabis purchase decisions like any other CPG product — driven by price, deals, and convenience — rather than needing an entirely unique retail model.

faq.question: What is Leafly and what problem does it solve for cannabis consumers?
faq.answer: Leafly is a cannabis media and marketplace platform focused on educating consumers and connecting them to retailers and brands; it helps people navigate an otherwise confusing, fragmented, state-by-state legal cannabis landscape by providing strain data, educational content, and menu information.

faq.question: Why is hemp-derived Delta-9 THC competing with licensed cannabis dispensaries?
faq.answer: Hemp-derived Delta-9 products are federally legal and can be shipped directly to consumers' homes across state lines, unlike state-licensed cannabis, which cannot cross state lines and is subject to heavier compliance costs — creating a similar consumer experience through very different regulatory channels.

faq.question: Why can't licensed cannabis retailers advertise easily on platforms like Instagram?
faq.answer: Because cannabis remains federally illegal, platforms like Meta enforce policies that can shut down accounts of plant-touching and even non-plant-touching cannabis businesses, even though unlicensed sellers often operate openly and unchecked on the same platforms.

faq.question: How does Leafly decide what content or products to cover?
faq.answer: Leafly uses a feedback loop combining input from retailers, brand partners, direct consumer submissions, and real-time search/behavioral data to identify trending topics, strains, and product categories worth covering.

faq.question: What role do budtenders play in the cannabis consumer journey?
faq.answer: Budtenders act as trusted intermediaries who help de-risk the intimidating experience of shopping for cannabis, guiding both new and experienced consumers toward products suited to their needs, which is why Leafly partners with and celebrates budtenders through initiatives like International Budtender Day.

faq.question: What was Leafly's role in New York's cannabis rollout?
faq.answer: Leafly partnered with the New York Cannabis Retailers Association (NYCRA) to help drive consumers toward licensed retailers, advocating for online ordering and delivery for licensed stores so they could compete with the convenience of illicit sellers.

faq.question: Are unlicensed online cannabis sellers being actively policed?
faq.answer: According to Yoko Miyashita, enforcement in markets like New York has focused more on physically padlocking unlicensed storefronts rather than actively pursuing unlicensed online ordering platforms, which remain a largely unaddressed gap.

faq.question: What consumer trend does Leafly's CEO predict will most shift attitudes toward cannabis?
faq.answer: Yoko Miyashita points to continued international and state-level legalization (citing Germany's 2024 move) as the key driver of stigma reduction, paired with ongoing consumer education at every stage of the buying journey.
